lesson.title: Why We Blame the Person, Not the Situation
lesson.summary: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to explain other people's behavior by pointing to their personality or character while underestimating the power of the situation they are in.
lesson.body:
Attribution theory says that whenever we observe someone's behavior, we automatically search for a cause, and we tend to sort possible causes into two broad categories: dispositional causes, something about the person's personality, ability, or character, and situational causes, something about the circumstances, pressures, or context surrounding the behavior. The fundamental attribution error, a term introduced by social psychologist Lee Ross in the late 1970s, names a very specific and very reliable bias in how people use those two categories. When explaining someone else's behavior, observers consistently lean toward dispositional explanations and underweight situational ones, even when the situational pressures are plain to see.

One of the clearest early demonstrations came from a study by Edward Jones and Victor Harris in 1967. Participants read essays that argued either for or against Fidel Castro's government, and they were told explicitly that the writer had been assigned that position by a debate coach and had no say in which side to argue. Even armed with that information, participants still rated the writer of the pro Castro essay as holding more genuinely pro Castro attitudes than the writer of the anti Castro essay. Knowing about an obvious situational constraint, an assigned position, did not stop people from reading the essay as a window into what the writer actually believed.

A related and often cited demonstration is the quiz game study Ross ran with Teresa Amabile and Julia Steinmetz in 1977. College students were randomly assigned to play either a quizmaster, who wrote difficult trivia questions drawn from their own knowledge, or a contestant, who tried to answer them. Because quizmasters could ask about whatever obscure things they personally happened to know, they naturally looked smart, and contestants naturally looked less knowledgeable by comparison, a built in situational advantage that had nothing to do with real intelligence. Observers watching the game were told exactly how the roles had been assigned, yet they still rated the quizmasters as more knowledgeable than the contestants in general, as though the role itself revealed something true about each person's underlying ability.

Why does this happen so reliably? Part of the answer is perceptual: when we watch someone act, that person is the vivid, moving, attention grabbing part of the scene, while the situational forces acting on them, rules, incentives, pressures, tend to fade into the background. We quite literally see the person more clearly than we see the forces shaping the person. Part of the answer is also cognitive convenience: a dispositional explanation is simple and stable and lets us stop thinking, "she's just rude" explains a lot at once, while a situational explanation usually requires more effortful reconstruction of context we cannot fully observe. This error shapes far more than lab studies. It affects how quickly we judge a stranger who snaps at us in traffic, how a manager reads an employee's missed deadline, and how a juror interprets a defendant's nervous demeanor, often without anyone pausing to weigh the situational pressures the other person was actually under.
